name: Danon disease
aliases: glycogen storage disease with normal acid maltase

reference.source: ESC/AHA cardiomyopathy guidelines; specialist inherited cardiomyopathy literature
clinicalPearls: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by variants in the LAMP2 gene, producing a triad of cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy and intellectual impairment
Affected males are usually severely affected and present early, often with a striking hypertrophic cardiomyopathy phenotype and ventricular pre-excitation
Female carriers are affected more variably and later, frequently with a dilated rather than hypertrophic pattern
Ventricular pre-excitation (a Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern) and very high QRS voltages are characteristic ECG clues
A mildly raised creatine kinase, subtle proximal weakness and retinal or visual abnormalities support the diagnosis
The disease is rapidly progressive in males, and cardiac transplantation is often required at a young age
Defibrillator therapy is considered because of the high arrhythmic and sudden death risk
Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis and enables screening of at-risk relatives
reference.pathophysiology: Danon disease is caused by variants in LAMP2, which encodes lysosome-associated membrane protein 2, a protein essential for autophagy and lysosomal function. Its deficiency impairs the fusion of autophagosomes with lysosomes, so autophagic vacuoles and glycogen accumulate within cardiac and skeletal muscle and other tissues. This storage and disrupted autophagy lead to progressive cardiomyocyte dysfunction and hypertrophy, conduction tissue involvement causing pre-excitation and arrhythmia, and skeletal muscle weakness. Because the gene is X-linked, hemizygous males are affected early and severely, while heterozygous females show a milder and later phenotype through variable X-inactivation.
additionalDifferentials: Pompe disease and other glycogen storage myopathies
Other causes of Wolff-Parkinson-White with left ventricular hypertrophy
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG for pre-excitation and high QRS voltages
Echocardiography and cardiac MRI to characterise hypertrophy, dilatation and fibrosis
Neurological and ophthalmological assessment for myopathy and retinopathy
redFlags: Rapidly progressive heart failure in a young male
Marked left ventricular hypertrophy with pre-excitation on ECG
Family history consistent with X-linked inheritance and early cardiac death
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is poor in affected males, with rapidly progressive cardiomyopathy and high arrhythmic risk often necessitating transplantation in adolescence or early adulthood; female carriers generally have a later and more variable course.
pitfalls: Labelling the cardiomyopathy as ordinary sarcomeric hypertrophic disease and missing the storage aetiology
Overlooking the diagnostic clues of pre-excitation, raised creatine kinase and mild myopathy
Underestimating disease severity and the need for early transplant assessment in males
Assuming female relatives are unaffected rather than at risk of later disease
Delaying genetic confirmation and family screening
references: ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiomyopathies
management: Manage under an inherited cardiac conditions service; with no established disease-specific drug, treatment targets the cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia
Treat the cardiomyopathy with standard heart-failure pharmacotherapy and monitor progression with serial echocardiography and cardiac MRI

Assess arrhythmic risk from ventricular pre-excitation and high-voltage cardiomyopathy, with electrophysiology review, implantable cardioverter-defibrillator in those at risk, and accessory-pathway ablation where indicated
Refer early for cardiac transplantation assessment given rapidly progressive heart failure, particularly in affected males
Screen for and manage skeletal myopathy and retinopathy with neurology and ophthalmology input
Offer genetic counselling for this X-linked LAMP2 disorder with cascade family screening, noting the milder, later phenotype in female carriers
Consider emerging gene-directed (AAV-based) therapy through specialist trial centres
